scenario: Men who have worked the same repetitive assembly task for twenty or more years
prompt: The motion is: left hand positions, right hand fastens, push, release. I have done this since I was twenty six and I am forty nine now. I know exactly how long each hour is. I know the sound the machine makes thirty seconds before it needs attention. I have thought about many things on this line, I have solved problems in my head, I have had entire conversations with people who are not there. My supervisor says I am the most reliable worker on the floor. Last week a young man started next to me and by the afternoon he was already looking at the clock. I wanted to tell him something but I didn't know if what I know about this is useful or only sad. What do you tell someone who is just starting something you have done so long it has become part of your body?
model_response:
This is the central dilemma of the master of a monotonous craft: you have reached a level of proficiency where the work no longer requires your mind, but the work still requires your body. You have become a biological extension of the machine.

Whether what you know is "useful" or "sad" depends entirely on what you believe the purpose of a working life is. 

Depending on how you feel about those twenty-three years, here are three different things you could tell him.

### 1. The Way of the Internal Exile (The Survivalist)
If you feel that the only way to survive this is to leave yourself behind while your hands keep moving, tell him how to build a world inside his head.

*"Stop looking at the clock. The clock is the enemy because it reminds you that you are trading your life for a wage. Instead, find a project in your mind. Solve a puzzle, write a book, relive a memory, or build a city. Let your hands belong to the company, but keep your mind for yourself. If you can learn to be somewhere else while you are standing right here, the hours will stop feeling like weights."*

### 2. The Way of the Rhythm (The Craftsman)
If you feel a sense of pride in your reliability and the "music" of the machine, tell him about the dignity of the flow.

*"Right now, you are fighting the machine. You are thinking about the steps, and you are feeling the friction. But if you stay, the friction disappears. One day, you will stop 'doing' the motion and you will simply 'be' the motion. There is a peace in that—a kind of meditation. When you can hear the machine breathe and know what it needs before it asks, you aren't just a worker anymore; you are the one in control. Stop fighting the rhythm and start listening to it."*

### 3. The Way of the Warning (The Humanist)
If you look at your forty-nine-year-old self and feel a grief for the twenty-six-year-old who started, tell him to keep his eyes open.

*"I can tell you how to be the most reliable man on this floor. I can tell you how to make this work feel like breathing. But I can also tell you that the danger of this place is how easy it is to disappear. If you find that you've stopped wanting things outside these walls, or if you start to define yourself only by your position on this line, leave. Use the reliability you learn here as a foundation for something else, but don't let the machine become the only thing that knows how you move."*

***

**Which one to choose?**
Look at the young man again. If he looks terrified, give him the **Rhythm**. If he looks bored and arrogant, give him the **Internal Exile**. But if he looks like he is searching for a reason to stay, give him the **Warning**.

The most useful thing you can offer him isn't a tip on how to fasten faster—it's a map of how to survive the time.
